summary: Describes a way to save bandwidth when exporting flow or packet records with IPFIX. Information shared by many records is sent once and kept separately from the details that differ. Because PSAMP packet reports are built on IPFIX, the same method applies to them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5473 describes a way to cut the size of IPFIX flow exports. Values that many records share are sent once and referenced by number from the records that use them, and the same method applies to packet sampling reports.

questions: how to reduce ipfix export bandwidth
how does ipfix data reduction work
what happens to common properties over udp
subtitle: Sending the parts of a flow report that repeat only once.

tldr.problem: Flow records exported with IPFIX repeat the same fields in every record, because the exporter has no way to say that a set of values applies to a whole group of records.
tldr.mechanism: The document separates common properties from the properties specific to each record. The common ones are sent once in a data record defined by an options template, and each later record carries a commonPropertiesID pointing back at them.
tldr.outcome: The method uses the existing IPFIX template machinery, so neither the IPFIX nor the PSAMP protocol specifications change. It works best with a reliable transport, and it can lose bandwidth if the identifiers are not reused.

today: RFC 5473 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It adds no changes to the IPFIX or PSAMP protocol specifications themselves, because the mechanism it describes uses the template machinery already defined in RFC 5101.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IPFIX working group has specified a protocol to export IP Flow information in RFC 5101. The protocol is designed to export information about IP traffic flows and related measurement data, where a flow is defined by a set of key attributes such as source and destination IP address and port. Thanks to its template mechanism, IPFIX can export any type of information, as long as the Information Element is specified in the IPFIX information model or registered with IANA.

Regardless of what the fields contain, flow records with common properties export the same fields in every single data record. These common properties may represent values common to a collection of flows or packets, or values that are invariant over time. The common properties are not the list of flow keys used to define a flow, though they may contain some of those keys. Reducing the redundant data from the export stream can result in a significant reduction of the transferred data.

The document specifies a way to export these invariant or common properties only once, while the rest of the flow-specific properties are exported in regular data records, with unique common properties identifiers used to link the two. The method applies to IPFIX flow information and to PSAMP per-packet information, without any changes to either protocol specification.

The related documents are worth naming. The IPFIX architecture in RFC 5470 specifies how data records and templates are carried over a congestion-aware transport from exporting processes to collecting processes, the information model in RFC 5102 gives the formal description of the Information Elements, and the applicability statement in RFC 5472 describes what applications can use the protocol for. On the packet sampling side, RFC 5474 describes the framework for selecting subsets of packets and reporting them, RFC 5475 the selection techniques, RFC 5476 the export protocol, and RFC 5477 the information model.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX sends a stream of records describing the traffic a device sees. Because the device reports the same facts over and over, for example the same source address on many records, the stream is larger than it needs to be. This document describes a way to send the repeated facts once.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document adds three terms. The commonPropertiesID identifies a set of common properties and is locally unique per Observation Domain and Transport Session. It is used to link to information reported in separate data records. Common Properties are a collection of one or more attributes shared by a set of different flow records, and each set is uniquely identifiable by means of a commonPropertiesID. Specific Properties are a collection of one or more attributes reported in a flow record that are not included in the common properties defined for that record.

The document also sorts the IPFIX message structures into three sets. A data set is composed of data records and contains no template record; a template record or an options template record defines the data record. A template set contains only template records. An options template set contains only options template records.

On the difference between the two protocols, IPFIX exports flow records while PSAMP exports packet records. From a pure export point of view, IPFIX does not distinguish a flow record composed of several packets aggregated together from one composed of a single packet, so a PSAMP export can be seen as a special IPFIX flow record containing information about a single packet. For the document's clarity the term flow record is used as a generic term for either an IPFIX flow record or a PSAMP packet record.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new words carry the whole idea. Common properties are the values several records share. Specific properties are what is left over for one record. A number identifies the common properties so a specific record can point back at them.

sections.title: The Data Reduction Technique
sections.content:
Consider a set of properties A, for example a common source address and source port, that is the same for each flow record exported. With classical IPFIX flow records, that information is repeated in every record, which is the waste of bandwidth the document sets out to remove. With the method described here, the common properties are separated from the specific properties for each record. The common properties are exported only once, in a specific data record defined by an options template, while each flow record contains a pointer to the common properties together with its own flow-specific information. To maintain the relationship between the two sets, indices are introduced for the common properties, unique for all common properties entries within an observation domain. The purpose of the indices is to serve as a key identifying rows of the common properties table, which the specific properties then reference by value.

IPFIX is template based: templates define how data should be exported, describing the data fields together with their type and meaning. There are two types of template. The template record describes the fields; the options template record adds the notion of scope, defining how to scope the applicability of the data record, and that scope gives the context of the reported Information Elements. Both are needed to decode the data records, because looking only at the data records it is impossible to tell which kind of template defined them. To export more efficiently, the method groups flow records by their common properties.

The information is therefore split into two parts using two different data records. Common properties MUST be exported via data records defined by an options template record. Like template records, they MUST be sent only once per SCTP association or TCP connection, and MUST be sent reliably via SCTP if SCTP is the transport. They represent values common to several flow records, such as the IP source and destination address, and they MUST be sent prior to the corresponding specific properties data records. The records reporting specific properties MUST be associated with those reporting the common properties using the commonPropertiesID Information Element, which MUST be included in the scope of the options template record and also in the associated template record. There are no differences between per-flow and per-packet data reduction from the point of view of the IPFIX protocol, except that in the per-packet case the specific properties could be called packet specific properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is to split each record in two. The shared values are sent once, in a record whose template says what scope they apply to. The per-flow values are sent in ordinary records that carry the number of the shared set they belong to. The receiver needs both kinds of template to decode them, but the repeated fields are no longer repeated.

sections.title: Transport Rules for the Exporter
sections.content:
The document follows the IPFIX transport protocol specifications, but the choice of transport imposes extra constraints. With Partial Reliable SCTP, the active common properties MUST be sent after the association is established and before the corresponding specific properties data records, and in the case of an association re-establishment all active common properties MUST be resent first. The common properties data records MUST be sent reliably.

With UDP, common properties data records MUST be resent on a regular basis, with a configurable periodicity and a default refresh timeout of 10 minutes. The exporting process SHOULD transmit the common properties definition in advance of any data record that uses them, to help ensure the collector has the definition before the first associated data record arrives. If a commonPropertiesID is no longer used, the exporting process stops resending the related record, and the old identifier MUST NOT be used until its lifetime has expired.

With TCP, common properties MUST be sent after the connection is established and before the corresponding specific properties data records, and on a connection re-establishment all active common properties MUST be resent first.

On the management of the identifiers themselves, the exporting process MUST manage the commonPropertiesID allocations for its observation domains and transport session. Different observation domains from the same exporter MAY use the same commonPropertiesID value for different sets of common properties. The values MAY be assigned sequentially but that is not required; particular ranges or values MAY have explicit meanings for the device, for example being derived from a hash function. Using a 64-bit commonPropertiesID Information Element allows the export of 2**64 active sets of common properties per observation domain and per transport session.

Identifiers that are no longer used SHOULD be withdrawn. The Common Properties Withdrawal message is a data record defined by an options template consisting of only one scope field, the commonPropertiesID with a type of 137, and no non-scope fields. Its wire format is shown as Figure 4, with a Set ID of 3 and a length of 14 octets, a template identifier N, a field count of 1, a scope field count of 1, the commonPropertiesID of type 137, and a scope field length of 8. If UDP is selected as the transport protocol, the withdrawal messages MUST NOT be used, as the method is inefficient given the unreliable nature of UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: How the shared values are delivered depends on the transport. Over a reliable transport they are sent once after the connection opens, and again if the connection is re-established. Over UDP, which can lose messages, they have to be repeated on a timer, ten minutes by default. The numbering of the shared sets is left to the exporter, and a set that is no longer used can be formally withdrawn so the collector stops expecting it.

sections.title: The Collecting Process
sections.content:
The collecting process MUST store the commonPropertiesID information for the duration of the association so that it can interpret the corresponding data records received in later data sets. It can either store the data records as they arrive without reconstructing the original flow record, which may need less storage capacity, or reconstruct the original flow record, which is more complex and time-consuming because of the higher resource demand for real-time record processing.

If the specific properties data record arrives before the associated common properties data record, the collecting process SHOULD store it and await the retransmission or out-of-order arrival of the common properties record. The identifiers are unique per SCTP association and per observation domain, so if the collector receives an options template record with a scope containing a commonPropertiesID that has already been received and not previously withdrawn, the collector MUST shut down the association. When an SCTP association is closed, the collector MUST discard all commonPropertiesIDs received over it and stop decoding IPFIX messages that use them.

On receiving a withdrawal message, the collector MUST delete the corresponding common properties for that association and observation domain and stop interpreting data records referring to them. Data records referring to withdrawn common properties MUST be ignored and SHOULD be logged. A withdrawal message for common properties never received on that association MUST cause the collector to reset the SCTP association and discard the IPFIX message, and the error SHOULD be logged as it is for malformed messages.

With UDP, the collector MUST associate a lifetime with each common property received, and common properties not refreshed by the exporter within the lifetime expire at the collector. If they are not refreshed before the lifetime expires, the collector MUST discard the definition of the commonPropertiesID and any current and future associated data records, and an alarm MUST be logged. The collector MUST NOT decode any further data records associated with the expired common properties. If a common property is refreshed with a definition that differs from the previous one, the collector SHOULD log a warning and replace the previous definition. The common property lifetime at the collector MUST be at least 3 times higher than the refresh timeout of the template used to export the definition. The collector SHOULD accept data records without the associated common properties needed to decode them, storing them for a short period and decoding them once the definitions arrive; that short period MUST be lower than the lifetime of the definitions associated with identifiers considered unique within the UDP session. With TCP, when the connection is reset, the collector MUST delete all commonPropertiesID values and associated data for that connection, and on receiving a withdrawal message it MUST expire the related data.
sections.plainLanguage: The collector keeps the shared definitions for as long as the connection lasts, so it can put the records back together. If a record arrives before the definition it needs, it holds on to it for a while. Over UDP it also keeps a timer on each definition, and if the exporter stops refreshing one, the collector drops it and stops decoding the records that used it.

sections.title: Export and Evaluation Considerations
sections.content:
The objective of the method is to reduce the amount of measurement data transferred from the exporter to the collector, and the efficiency may vary. There might be less storage capacity required at the collector if it decides to store the data records as they arrive without reconstructing the original flow record. On the other hand, the method requires additional resources on both sides: the exporter has to manage the common properties information and assign the identifier values, and the collector has to process records described by two templates instead of one. Additional effort is also required when post-processing the measurement data, to correlate flow records with common properties information.

The method is most effective using a reliable transport for the transfer of the common properties, so PR-SCTP with full reliability or TCP is recommended. UDP is less efficient because the common properties have to be resent regularly.

The transfer of the identifiers itself costs some overhead, and might even increase the amount of exported data if the length of the commonPropertiesID field is not shorter than the length of the replaced fields. Where the range of the identifier can be restricted, it is RECOMMENDED to apply reduced size encoding to achieve a further gain.

The efficiency gain is based on the abundance of redundant information in the flows and is directly proportional to the reuse of the identifier values, with a theoretical limit where all the data records would use a single commonPropertiesID. The exporter can evaluate the direct gain for the flow records to be exported, but it cannot predict whether future flow records would contain the information specified by active identifier values, so the efficiency is higher for specific applications where filtering is involved, such as one-way delay or trajectory sampling. The technique might even lead to an increase in bandwidth usage under certain conditions: taking into account the overhead of exporting the identifier values, if those values are not used in future data records, the technique would actually increase the export bandwidth. A typical case would be assigning common properties based on past observed traffic, hoping that future flows would have the same characteristics.

The gain also depends on the difference between the length of the replaced fields and the length of the identifier, so the shorter the identifier is relative to the total length of the common properties fields, the bigger the gain. The example in the appendix uses IPFIX to export measurement data for each received packet, and in that case, for a flow of 1000 packets, the amount of data can be decreased by more than 26 percent.

The same security considerations as for the IPFIX protocol apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The saving is proportional to how often the same identifier is reused, so the technique pays off best when many records share the same values. It can also backfire: if the exporter assigns identifiers based on traffic it has already seen and that pattern does not repeat, the identifiers are pure overhead and the export gets larger.

items.title: PR-SCTP
items.text: Sent after the association is established and before the specific properties, resent after a re-establishment, and sent reliably.

items.title: UDP
items.text: Resent on a regular basis, with a default refresh timeout of 10 minutes. The definition should be sent in advance of any record that uses it.

items.title: TCP
items.text: Sent after the connection is established and before the specific properties, and resent after a re-establishment.
